articles.title: Global Government Bond Yields Hit Multi-Decade Highs
articles.dek: See why global bond yields are at multi-decade highs, what's driving rising Treasury yields, how higher interest rates affect stocks and consumers, and more.
points: Global bond yields have surged to multi-decade highs, with the U.S. 10-year Treasury, U.K. 30-year gilt, French 10-year and Japanese 10-year government bond all hitting levels unseen in more than 20 years.
An increase in projected rate hikes, elevated energy prices and sticky inflation amid a backdrop of healthy labor markets and growth have driven the spike in yields in the U.S. and Europe.
Higher yields risk being self-reinforcing, with tighter credit and pricier borrowing feeding larger deficits.
The squeeze from high yields threatens both equities and consumers, with equity-yield correlations growing more fragile and consumers facing higher APRs on car loans, mortgages and other credit.

articles.title: AI Capex & Hyperscaler Investment Outlook
articles.dek: AI capital expenditures are projected to approach a trillion dollars. How big will it get, and how long will it last?
points: J.P. Morgan Global Research projects global spending on AI capex to reach $5.5 trillion by 2030 and for $900 billion to be spent in 2026 alone.

Revenue from cloud service providers has become the most salient data supporting the investment thesis for AI capex, with revenue run-rates showing year-over-year gains and future contracted revenues projecting solid growth.
The shift in financing from free cash flow to debt, including bond and equity raises, offers a clear window into investor appetite to fund AI capex.
Bottlenecks ranging from memory and GPU supply to permitting and public opinion represent real challenges to the pace and profitability of AI capex.

articles.title: Business Checkpoint: Looking into the logistics
articles.dek: Profitability growth was positive in the third quarter, but logistics costs and supply chain pressures are creating challenges.
points: Small and mid-sized businesses entered Q3 in relatively solid financial condition, with profitability growth up across both groups, according to Bank of America business account data. Nearly half of estimated tariff payments had been refunded by September, though the share of these refunds relative to revenue has peaked.

In Bank of America business payments data, logistics spending growth per client was up four times as much for small than midsized firms. Additionally, distribution and inventory transactions growth per client has outpaced spending since the spring of 2025.

Growing transportation bottlenecks are re-emerging ahead of the holiday season. Trucking capacity has tightened as driver availability remains constrained, according to BofA Global Research. This has pushed freight rates higher and driven strong transportation sector payroll growth, particularly among mid-sized businesses, according to Bank of America payments data.

articles.title: The Long Road Home: Examining the Global Housing Affordability Crisis
articles.dek: Chronic supply-demand imbalances, elevated mortgage rates and rising ownership costs are straining housing affordability across many markets — a global problem that demands localized solutions.
points: Despite unprecedented wealth gains, housing affordability in the U.S. is at multi-decade lows, with factors including tight inventory and high mortgage rates pricing buyers out of the market.
Recent U.S. policy actions such as the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act and the purchase of agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) have provided limited relief.
Beyond the U.S., housing affordability is very much a global story. For instance, China remains in a prolonged housing reset, while affordable housing is losing market share in India.

articles.title: Consumer Checkpoint: Strength in numbers
articles.dek: September saw solid spending across many categories and a strong start to the holidays.
points: Consumer spending remained very solid in September. Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card spending per household rose 6.2% year-over-year (YoY), or 5.1% excluding gasoline, both the third strongest growth rates over the past four years. Month-over-month (MoM) spending was more muted, especially without gas.

Spending shows considerable breadth: the vast majority of discretionary retail and services categories are showing growth. Moreover, this strength extends across income cohorts, with the ongoing recovery of lower- and middle-income households' spending growth.

With the winter months fast approaching, holiday spending is already increasing at a solid rate, though it's still early. In Bank of America deposit data through September, buy now, pay later (BNPL) usage is rising but not at a rate that is overly concerning. However, nearly one in every five households that use BNPL has a repayment of over $500.

articles.title: The Institute Employment Report: September 2026
articles.dek: Bank of America Institute analysis shows slower payroll growth, declining unemployment payments and continued strength in lower-income wage growth.
points: Job growth softened further in September, according to Bank of America's deposit data, with growth of 1.4% year-over-year (YoY), from 1.5% in August. But falling unemployment payments in September indicate a relatively healthy overall picture.

Lower-income households' wage growth remains strongest, despite a narrowing gap. After-tax wage growth eased to 4.5% YoY for lower-income households in September, while rising to 3.8% and 3.7% for middle- and higher-income households, respectively.

Lower tax withholdings and a relative strengthening in the younger/lower-income end of the labor market are driving this story. Additionally, average hours have risen in some lower-paid industries, which is also boosting pay packets.

articles.title: Fundamentally, higher borrowing costs make it less attractive to finance new assets
articles.dek: From a sentiment standpoint, REITs are sometimes viewed as bond proxies, so higher yields pressure share prices. Higher bond yields have created headwinds for Real Estate, one of the most rate-sensitive sectors of the stock market.

articles.title: SMID-Cap Outlook: The Revival Looks Set to Continue
articles.dek: The stock market is broadening as investors rotate away from the crowded mega-cap space and into the small- and mid-cap universe. What’s driving this shift?
points: Small- and mid-cap (SMID) stocks are rebounding, with the Russell 2500 Index outpacing larger-cap benchmarks like the S&P 500.
This dynamic is playing out in developed markets (DM); conversely, SMID caps have underperformed in emerging markets (EM) year to date.

J.P. Morgan Global Research expects the SMID-cap revival to continue in the short term thanks to five reasons: improving fundamentals, depressed positioning, trough technicals, geopolitical tailwinds and record valuation discounts.

articles.title: Economic Impact of Iran Conflict on Oil, Gold and More
articles.dek: With $100/bbl crude, commodities markets are repricing risk in real time — with some surprising results.
points: The U.S.–Israel military operation against Iran has led to dramatic seesaws in oil markets, with Brent crude prices elevated for much of the year.

Gold’s status as a safe haven has been tested during the Iran conflict, though J.P. Morgan Global Research believes structural drivers — including central bank buying and broader de-dollarization — are still intact.

As with oil, aluminum prices could be affected by the status of the Strait of Hormuz following attacks on key Middle Eastern smelters, with an “invisible” aluminum deficit potentially working its way through the supply chain.
Overall, the conflict’s effect on global growth may prove less severe than initially feared, with J.P. Morgan economists expressing cautious optimism that a cyclical upturn could continue.
